paragraphs.heading: Balance and how steady it is
paragraphs.text: A particle is in mechanical equilibrium when the forces acting on it cancel out, leaving a net force of zero. A bigger system built from many pieces counts as balanced when each piece has zero net force on it. Once something is balanced, an important question is how steady that balance is. That property is called stability, and balanced states can be stable, unstable or neutral.

paragraphs.heading: The low point of a dip
paragraphs.text: In a stable equilibrium, the potential energy of the system sits at a local minimum, like the low point of a dip. Give the system a small push and the forces that arise tend to bring the balance back. A local minimum of this kind marks a stable equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: Unstable and neutral cases
paragraphs.text: The reverse happens when the potential energy is at a local maximum. That balance is unstable: shift the system even a tiny distance and its own forces carry it farther off. A third kind is neutral, where a small shift leaves the system nearly in balance. In a truly neutral state the energy does not change, and the balance holds over a finite width. People also call this marginal stability, a state of indifference, or astable equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: Metastable states and directions
paragraphs.text: Some systems have more than one stable resting state. Any of those whose potential energy is above the lowest possible value is called metastable. Direction matters too: a system can hold steady against shifts along one axis yet tip away along another, an arrangement known as a saddle point. So a balance is normally called stable only when it is stable in every direction.

paragraphs.heading: Testing with derivatives
paragraphs.text: To judge stability precisely, higher order derivatives can be checked. If the lowest derivative that is not zero has even order and a positive value, the balance is stable; if it has odd order or a negative value, it is unstable. When every derivative is zero, the derivatives alone settle nothing. The function e^(−1/x²), set to 0 at x=0, is an example: all its derivatives vanish, yet it has a local minimum at x=0 and so is a stable equilibrium. Multiply it by the Sign function and the derivatives stay zero, but the balance turns unstable.

paragraphs.heading: A shape with one way to rest
paragraphs.text: Stability also raises a puzzle about solid shapes resting under gravity on a flat surface. For uniform, convex bodies, the smallest possible number of balanced resting positions is of special interest. A flat, two-dimensional shape needs at least 4. In three dimensions, though, an object can be made with only one stable and one unstable balance point, and such an object is called a gömböc.
